title: Where the salt actually is
standfirst: Most of it is not from the shaker. Most of it does not taste salty.

spans.text: Ask someone where they get their salt and they will point at crisps, or at the shaker on the table. Both are small parts of the answer.
Most sodium in the diet arrives in packaged and prepared food, before anyone reaches for a shaker.
And the biggest single source is not a snack. Bread and rolls lead the list, ahead of anything you would think of as salty.
Salt does more than season bread. It slows the yeast, tightens the dough and keeps the loaf from going stale as fast. A loaf can carry a lot of it and taste of none.
That is the trap: taste is a poor guide here. Cheese, cold cuts, soup and sandwiches all sit near the top of the list for the same reason.
The useful move is not to eat less bread. It is to notice that bread is a place where brands differ a lot, and that the difference is invisible until you look.
The categories worth checking are the boring ones. You already check the crisps.

blocks.action: I will compare the sodium before I pick a loaf

spans.text: Sodium content varies widely between brands in the same category, so a rule of thumb about a whole food group will be wrong as often as it is right. The number on the pack is the only reliable version.
